GitHub Actions can automatically build and publish our `vetiver` models to our S3 whenever we push changes to a specific branch (we covered these in [Lab 5](lab05.qmd) and [GitHub Actions as CI/CD](publish-r-py.qmd)). I've stored the Quarto files for building, pushing, and pulling the model data in the [`_labs/lab07/` folder](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs/tree/main/_labs/lab07). 

In this section I'll cover connecting GitHub to AWS with OpenID Connect (OIDC) and creating a workflow to automate the model publishing process.

## Automating Model Deployment with GitHub Actions

The workflow needs AWS credentials to write to S3. We could store the `mjfrigaard-cli` access key in the repository's secrets, but that key can do much more than this workflow needs. It carries every permission in `dev-deploy-group` (including `AmazonEC2FullAccess` and `IAMFullAccess`), it never expires, and our local `dev-deploy` profile uses the same key. If the secret leaked, someone could launch instances or create IAM users. Rotating the key ([Rotating access keys](start-aws.qmd#rotating-access-keys)) would also mean updating the laptop and GitHub at the same time.

OIDC avoids storing a key at all. Each workflow run asks GitHub for a signed token that names the repository and branch it's running from. AWS checks the token and hands back temporary credentials for an IAM role, and those credentials expire after an hour. The role can only write to the model bucket, and only this repository's `lab07-s3` branch can assume it.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: 'GitHub OIDC and AWS'
%%| fig-width: 7.0
%%| fig-align: 'center'
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace'}}}%%

graph TD
    Run(["<strong>Workflow Run</strong><br/><em>(lab07-s3)</em>"])
    Token("<strong>GitHub OIDC Token</strong><br/><em>repo + branch</em>")
    STS("<strong>AWS STS</strong><br/><em>checks trust policy</em>")
    Role("<strong>gha-s3-publish-role</strong>")
    Creds("Temporary AWS<br/>Credentials (1 hour)")
    Access[("Access to S3")]

    Run --"requests"--> Token
    Token --"AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity"--> STS
    STS --> Role
    Role --> Creds
    Creds --> Access

    style Run fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff
    style Token fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff
    style STS fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff
    style Role fill:#D2562B,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff
    style Creds fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff
    style Access fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff
```

Setting this up takes three steps in AWS (an identity provider, a role, and a permissions policy) and two repository variables. The AWS commands use the `dev-deploy` profile, which has `IAMFullAccess` from [Stand up an EC2 instance](aws-ec2.qmd).

### Adding GitHub as an identity provider

First we tell IAM to trust tokens signed by GitHub. We only do this once per AWS account:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider \
  --url https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --client-id-list sts.amazonaws.com \
  --profile dev-deploy
```

The output is the provider's ARN:

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
{
    "OpenIDConnectProviderArn": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
}
```

:::

### Creating the role

The role's trust policy decides who can assume it. Store the account ID in a shell variable, then write the policy to `trust-policy.json`. Type `ACCOUNT_ID` exactly as written (don't replace it with your account number), because the shell fills in the number for us. Run both commands in the same Terminal session from the repository root:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity \
  --query Account --output text \
  --profile dev-deploy)

cat > trust-policy.json <<EOF
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::${ACCOUNT_ID}:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs:ref:refs/heads/lab07-s3"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
EOF
```

Confirm the shell filled in the account ID by searching the file for the `Federated` line:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
grep Federated trust-policy.json
```

The ARN should contain the 12 digit account ID:

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
```

:::

If the ARN shows `arn:aws:iam:::oidc-provider` (nothing between the colons), `ACCOUNT_ID` wasn't set in this shell. Run the `ACCOUNT_ID=` line again and rewrite the file.

The `aud` condition checks that the token was issued for AWS. The `sub` condition limits the role to pushes on the `lab07-s3` branch of this repository, so a workflow in any other repository (or on another branch) can't assume it.

Create the role from the trust policy:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
aws iam create-role \
  --role-name gha-s3-publish-role \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json \
  --profile dev-deploy
```

The output includes the role's ARN (`arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/gha-s3-publish-role`), which goes in the repository below.

```{r}
#| label: co_box_less_pager
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| eval: true
co_box(
  color = "b",
  look = "default",
  hsize = "1.25",
  size = "1.00",
  header = "AWS Pager Output",
  fold = FALSE,
  contents = "
The output repeats because the AWS CLI sends long output through a pager (`less`), and each scroll redrew it. Press `q` to get back to the prompt. To turn the pager off for this session, run:

\`\`\`bash
export AWS_PAGER=\"\"
\`\`\`

")
```


### Limiting the role to the model bucket

The new role has no permissions. `pins` lists, reads, and writes objects in the bucket, so the permissions policy allows those three actions on `penguin-vetiver-model-data` and nothing else:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
cat > s3-publish-policy.json <<EOF
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::penguin-vetiver-model-data"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::penguin-vetiver-model-data/*"
    }
  ]
}
EOF

aws iam put-role-policy \
  --role-name gha-s3-publish-role \
  --policy-name s3-publish \
  --policy-document file://s3-publish-policy.json \
  --profile dev-deploy
```

`ListBucket` applies to the bucket itself, while `GetObject` and `PutObject` apply to the objects inside it (the `/*`). `put-role-policy` returns no output on success, so we check the role directly. `list-role-policies` lists the policies attached to the role:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
aws iam list-role-policies \
  --role-name gha-s3-publish-role \
  --profile dev-deploy
```

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
{
    "PolicyNames": [
        "s3-publish"
    ]
}
```

:::

`get-role-policy` returns the policy itself, so we can confirm the actions and the bucket:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
aws iam get-role-policy \
  --role-name gha-s3-publish-role \
  --policy-name s3-publish \
  --profile dev-deploy
```

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
{
    "RoleName": "gha-s3-publish-role",
    "PolicyName": "s3-publish",
    "PolicyDocument": {
        "Version": "2012-10-17",
        "Statement": [
            {
                "Effect": "Allow",
                "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
                "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::penguin-vetiver-model-data"
            },
            {
                "Effect": "Allow",
                "Action": [
                    "s3:GetObject",
                    "s3:PutObject"
                ],
                "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::penguin-vetiver-model-data/*"
            }
        ]
    }
}
```

:::

IAM now keeps its own copy of each policy, so we can delete the two JSON files:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
rm trust-policy.json s3-publish-policy.json
```

### Setting up GitHub Variables

The workflow reads two values from the repository (**Settings** > **Secrets and variables** > **Actions** > **Variables**). Neither one is sensitive. The role ARN is useless outside the repository and branch named in the trust policy:

1. `AWS_ROLE_ARN`: the ARN of `gha-s3-publish-role`
2. `AWS_REGION`: AWS region (e.g., `us-east-1`)

We can set both from the Terminal with the GitHub CLI (in the same shell, so `ACCOUNT_ID` is still set):

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
gh variable set AWS_ROLE_ARN \
  --body "arn:aws:iam::${ACCOUNT_ID}:role/gha-s3-publish-role"
```

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
✓ Created variable AWS_ROLE_ARN for mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs
```

:::

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
gh variable set AWS_REGION --body "us-east-1"
```


::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
✓ Updated variable AWS_REGION for mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs
```

:::

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
gh variable list
```

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
NAME          VALUE                                             UPDATED
AWS_REGION    us-east-1                                         less than a minute ago
AWS_ROLE_ARN  arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/gha-s3-publish-role  about 1 minute ago
```

:::

The repository doesn't need any AWS secrets. If it still has `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` from an earlier setup, delete them after the first successful run with the role:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
gh secret delete AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
```

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
gh secret delete AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
```

If a secret doesn't exist, `gh secret delete` returns a 404 error:

::: {style="font-style: italic;"}

```{verbatim}
failed to delete secret AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: HTTP 404 (https://api.github.com/repos/mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs/actions/secrets/AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID)
```

:::

The 404 means there's nothing to delete, so we can ignore it. `gh secret list` confirms the repository has no secrets left (it prints nothing):

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
gh secret list
```

### GitHub Actions Workflow File

Next, we create `.github/workflows/publish.yml`[^gha-workflow] to build and publish the models to our S3 bucket. The models are automatically versioned by `vetiver` (e.g., `20260710T065220Z-91fdd`), so we're creating a new version in S3 with each workflow run.

```{.yaml}
name: Publish Models to S3

on:
  push:
    branches: [lab07-s3] #<1>
    paths:
      - '_labs/lab07/py_model.qmd'
      - '_labs/lab07/r_model.qmd'
      - '.github/workflows/publish.yml'

permissions: #<2>
  id-token: write
  contents: read #<2>

jobs:
  publish-models:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Check out repository #<3>
        uses: actions/checkout@v4 #<3>

      - name: Configure AWS credentials #<4>
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: ${{ vars.AWS_REGION || 'us-east-1' }} #<4>

      - name: Set up Python #<5>
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'

      - name: Set up R
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: '4.4'
          use-public-rspm: true

      - name: Set up Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Install Python dependencies
        working-directory: ./_labs/lab07
        run: |
          python -m pip install --upgrade pip
          pip install -r Python/requirements.txt pins vetiver python-dotenv s3fs jupyter "setuptools<81"

      - name: Install R dependencies
        working-directory: ./_labs/lab07
        run: |
          R -e "install.packages(c('vetiver', 'pins', 'plumber2', 'paws.storage', 'palmerpenguins', 'duckdb', 'DBI', 'dplyr', 'rmarkdown', 'knitr'))" #<5>

      - name: Build and publish Python model #<6>
        working-directory: ./_labs/lab07
        env:
          USE_S3: 'true'
          AWS_REGION: ${{ vars.AWS_REGION || 'us-east-1' }}
          PINS_ALLOW_PICKLE_READ: '1'
        run: |
          quarto render py_model.qmd

      - name: Build and publish R model
        working-directory: ./_labs/lab07
        env:
          USE_S3: 'true'
          AWS_REGION: ${{ vars.AWS_REGION || 'us-east-1' }}
        run: |
          quarto render r_model.qmd #<6>
          
```
1. **Trigger**: Runs when `py_model.qmd`, `r_model.qmd`, or this workflow file changes on the `lab07-s3` branch
2. **Permissions**: `id-token: write` lets the job request an OIDC token from GitHub. Setting `permissions` removes the defaults, so `contents: read` keeps checkout working  
3. **Checkout**: Downloads the latest code from the repository  
4. **AWS Auth**: Uses `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` to trade the OIDC token for temporary credentials from `gha-s3-publish-role`  
5. **Setup**: Installs Python 3.12, R 4.4, Quarto, and the required dependencies  
6. **Build & Publish**: Renders `py_model.qmd` and `r_model.qmd` with the `USE_S3=true` environment variable, which causes the model code to write directly to S3

The workflow renders the same `.qmd` files we render locally, so there are no separate scripts to keep in sync.

The `use-public-rspm: true` option in the **Set up R** step points R at the [Posit Public Package Manager](https://p3m.dev/), which serves prebuilt Linux binaries. Without it, `install.packages()` compiles every R package from source, and the first successful run of this workflow took about 25 minutes (most of it in **Install R dependencies**).

Publishing with GitHub Actions automates the model deployment without storing any AWS credentials in the repository.


[^gha-workflow]: Note that file is stored in the [root directory (`.github/workflows/`)](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs/tree/main/.github/workflows)--where all workflow files belong.

## Developing on the `lab07-s3` Branch

Because I want the `main` branch reserved for the Quarto book rendering, I'll create and check out a `lab07-s3` branch from `main` for model changes (pushing to this branch triggers the model publishing workflow):

```{bash}
#| eval: false 
#| code-fold: false 
git checkout -b lab07-s3
```

And push the new branch to GitHub:

```{bash}
#| eval: false 
#| code-fold: false
git push -u origin lab07-s3
```

Once on the `lab07-s3` branch, I'll need to follow this process:

### Make changes 

Make changes to the model files (i.e., [`_labs/lab07/py_model.qmd`](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs/blob/main/_labs/lab07/py_model.qmd) or [`_labs/lab07/r_model.qmd`](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/do4ds-labs/blob/main/_labs/lab07/r_model.qmd))

### Test changes (locally)

To test changes locally, I'll need to set the environment variables for S3 (or use local for testing):

```{bash}
#| eval: false 
#| code-fold: false
export USE_S3=false  # or true if testing S3 locally
```

Then render/run the files with the changes

```{bash}
#| eval: false 
#| code-fold: false
quarto render py_model.qmd
```

Or

```{bash}
#| eval: false 
#| code-fold: false
quarto render r_model.qmd
```

### Commit changes 

Commit the changes (be specific about the files):

```{bash}
#| eval: false 
#| code-fold: false
git add _labs/lab07/py_model.qmd _labs/lab07/r_model.qmd
git commit -m "Update model configuration or training logic"
```

### Push changes 

Push to the `lab07-s3` branch:

```{bash}
#| eval: false 
#| code-fold: false
git push origin lab07-s3
```


GitHub Actions will automatically detect the `push` to `lab07-s3`, build the models using the latest code, and publish the versioned models to S3 with temporary credentials from `gha-s3-publish-role`. 

### Verify

The GitHub CLI (`gh`) lets us follow the workflow from the Terminal. First, list the most recent runs of `publish.yml`. Each row shows the status, the commit message, the branch, the run ID, and how long the run took:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
gh run list --workflow publish.yml --limit 2
```

Pass the run ID from that list to `gh run watch` to follow the run until it finishes. The `--exit-status` flag makes the command fail when the run fails, so we don't have to read the output to know the result:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
gh run watch <run-id> --exit-status
```

To see where the time goes, `gh api` requests the run's jobs from the GitHub REST API (`{owner}` and `{repo}` are filled in from the current repository). The `--jq` filter prints each step's name and how many seconds it took. The **Install R dependencies** step should take about a minute with `use-public-rspm: true` (compiling from source took most of the 25 minute first run):

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/<run-id>/jobs \
  --jq '.jobs[0].steps[] | "\(.name): \(((.completed_at|fromdate)-(.started_at|fromdate)))s"'
```

We can also confirm R downloaded its packages from Package Manager by searching the run's log for its address (`packagemanager.posit.co`). The `__linux__` part of each URL means Package Manager sends a prebuilt binary for the runner's Linux version:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
gh run view <run-id> --log | grep -m3 "packagemanager.posit.co"
```

Finally, we verify the models were published by listing the files in the bucket. Each run adds a new version folder (named with the date and time, e.g., `20261106T183259Z-6a79d`) under `Python/models/penguin_lab07_model/` and `R/models/penguin_lab07_model/`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
# List files in S3
aws s3 ls s3://penguin-vetiver-model-data/ --recursive --profile dev-deploy
```

### Merge to `main`

Then switch back to the `main` branch:

```{bash}
#| eval: false 
#| code-fold: false
git checkout main
```

This will merge the changes in `lab07-s3` to `main` (if the changes also belong in the book).

```{bash}
#| eval: false 
#| code-fold: false
git merge lab07-s3
```

Push changes to `main`.

```{bash}
#| eval: false 
#| code-fold: false
git push origin main
```

Then publish the book:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
quarto publish gh-pages
```

## Recap

1. GitHub authenticates to AWS with OIDC instead of an access key. We added GitHub as an identity provider and created `gha-s3-publish-role`, which only the `lab07-s3` branch of this repository can assume and which can only list, read, and write objects in the model bucket. The role ARN and `AWS_REGION` go in the repository's Variables, and each run gets credentials that expire after an hour.

2. `publish.yml` runs on pushes to the `lab07-s3` branch that change `py_model.qmd`, `r_model.qmd`, or the workflow file itself. It installs Python and R, then renders both model documents with `USE_S3=true`, so each run writes a new `vetiver` version to S3.

3. Model changes happen on `lab07-s3` (make changes, test locally, commit, push, and verify with `aws s3 ls`), which keeps `main` reserved for rendering the book. Changes that also belong in the book get merged back into `main`.

[Lab 8](lab08.qmd) moves to the command line and how SSH keys work.
